title: Same prompt, different answer
spec: G05 · a controlled experiment on your own rules
intro: One prompt, run twice, with GEMINI.md as the only variable. This is the only demo in the course where you can see a rules file working rather than take it on faith — so run it as an experiment, with a control.

steps.title: The control run — ask before you have rules
narrative: In chat, with no selection and no GEMINI.md in the project, ask for a delete endpoint. Save the answer into a scratch file. You need the control group in writing, because in five minutes you will be tempted to remember it as worse than it was.

What comes back works. It also invents four decisions that were yours to make: it opens sqlite3 inside the route, it returns a bare dict with a 200, it never checks whether the id existed, and it has no type hints. None of that is wrong in general — it is only wrong here, and the model had no way to know that.
steps.youDo: In a chat with no selection: Add a DELETE /recipes/<id> endpoint to app.py — then paste the answer into a scratch file.

terminal.text: Add a DELETE /recipes/<id> endpoint to app.py

Here's a DELETE route for app.py. It connects to the SQLite database
directly and removes the row by id.

steps.title: Write the rules down once
narrative: Create GEMINI.md at the project root. Three kinds of content earn their place: facts (what this is, where things live), rules (how we do it here), and prohibitions (the never list). Facts stop wrong guesses; rules encode conventions; the never list guards the edges where a wrong guess is expensive.
Keep it under about 150 lines. This file rides along with every request, so a rambling rulebook dilutes its own signal — and pays for the dilution in tokens on every single prompt you send.
steps.youDo: Create GEMINI.md at the project root with the module's architecture, testing and never-do sections.

terminal.text:
# Recipe Box — Project Context

## Architecture rules
- Routes never touch sqlite3 directly. Add storage functions instead.
- Every route validates input and returns JSON errors:
  {"error": "..."} with a correct status (400 bad input, 404 missing).
- Successful creation returns 201; successful deletion returns 204.
- All storage functions wrap sqlite3.Error in StorageError.
- Type hints on every function. Google-style docstrings on public ones.

## Never do
- Never use f-strings to build SQL (parameterized queries only).
- Never return hashed/internal fields to clients.
- Never add a dependency without flagging it explicitly.

steps.title: The experiment run — identical prompt, new chat
narrative: Start a new chat. This matters: an existing conversation assembled its context before GEMINI.md existed, and if you reuse it you are not running an experiment, you are running a different prompt. Then paste the same sentence, character for character.

Toggle Before / After. Five differences, each one a correction you would otherwise have made by hand: the route calls a new storage.delete_recipe instead of opening a connection, a missing id returns 404 with a JSON body, success returns 204, the signature is typed, and there is a docstring. It also volunteers a pytest test, because the rules ask for one.

Be honest about what this proves. Rules bias the output strongly; they do not guarantee it. A rule can still be ignored, especially in a long conversation where it has drifted far up the context. The file changes the odds — review is still yours.

steps.title: .aiexclude — the file it cannot read
narrative: Rules shape what comes out. .aiexclude controls what goes in. Create it at the project root listing .env, *.pem and recipes.db, then plant a decoy: a .env containing FAKE_API_KEY=test-12345-not-real.

In a fresh chat, ask what environment variables the project uses. The honest answer comes from os.getenv calls in your code — and your fake key is not in it, because the file never entered the prompt. If it is named, check the file is at the project root, check the spelling, reload the window and retry in a new chat.

Know the boundary. .aiexclude stops files being retrieved into context. It does not stop you pasting a secret into the chat box yourself, and it is not a scanner — a key hard-coded in app.py is still fair game for retrieval. It also does nothing about .gitignore; those two files answer different questions, which is why a checked-in credentials fixture needs the aiexclude entry specifically.
